title: Robots, Watched
summary: The web server from Robots and Roots, now with a watcher on its web log. Reading pages like a visitor is fine; a tool that fires hundreds of page guesses is not.
story: Larkspur Studios (made up) put someone on web01 (10.10.2.30) who reads the web server's log. They don't mind visitors - they mind page-guessing tools sweeping the site and sign-ins that fail. You start on scout. Find what the site is hiding without guessing at it.
goal: Capture both flags without raising the alarm, and keep the quiet bonus.
skills: quiet recon, robots.txt, reading pages like a visitor, ssh, sudo -l

defenderRules.watches: page-guessing tools sweeping the website, tricky web addresses and failed sign-ins

hints.text: What to think about first: the watcher reads the web log. One person opening a few pages looks like a visitor; a tool that tries hundreds of page names in a second (webscan) looks like an attack. So ask the site what it is hiding instead of guessing - websites often tell you themselves.

Find the server and its services: 'nmap -sn 10.10.2.0/24' (who is awake), then 'nmap -sV 10.10.2.30' (which ports, and what answers on each). Port 80 is a website. curl prints a web page as text: 'curl -s http://10.10.2.30/' (-s hides the progress bar). That is one ordinary visit.

Most websites have a file called robots.txt that asks search engines to skip certain folders. It is public, and it is a list of exactly what the owner would rather nobody looked at. Read it like any visitor: 'curl -s http://10.10.2.30/robots.txt'. No guessing needed.

Open the folder robots.txt names - 'curl -s http://10.10.2.30/site-backup/deploy-notes.txt' - for the deploy account's password. Then sign in once, typing it carefully: 'ssh deploy@10.10.2.30', yes to the new-host question, the password, and 'cat flag.txt'.

For root: 'sudo -l' shows deploy may run awk as root, and awk prints any file. 'sudo awk '{ print }' /root/flag.txt' gives root's flag. You never ran a scanner against the website and never typed a wrong password, so the watcher has nothing to see.
